title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.

reading.body:
The core failure here is a data-sourcing decision made before deployment. Suno admitted its model was trained on essentially all music files on the internet, and reporting based on a hack identified YouTube, Deezer, and Genius among the scraped sources. That training material included copyrighted recordings obtained without license or permission. The failure is not in the model's inference behavior alone but in the composition of the training corpus, a decision made upstream of any user interaction.

The outputs then compounded the problem at the deployment layer. When prompted with specific stylistic cues, the systems produced audio that closely replicated distinctive melodies, rhythms, and in at least one case original lyrics from named recordings. That is a model reproducing protected expression rather than generating novel content, which is a distinct failure from a system simply trained on copyrighted data. No rights-clearance check or output filter appears to have been in place to catch reproduction before it reached users.

What the litigation has established varies by jurisdiction. A German court ruled against Suno in the GEMA case, and a US court denied Suno's motion to dismiss artists' claims. Warner Music settled with Suno and entered a joint venture, and Universal Music settled with Udio. The allegations of deliberate concealment of training data sources and intentional infringement are claims made in legal filings, not findings of fact, and the remaining cases have not been adjudicated.

summary:
Major record labels including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, and Warner Music have filed separate lawsuits against AI music generators Udio and Suno, alleging they scraped thousands of copyrighted songs without permission to train their models. The labels claim both companies deliberately concealed which music they used for training and argue that the companies' business model fundamentally relies on copyright infringement. The record labels submitted thousands of specific songs they say were copied, including works by The Beatles, Frank Sinatra, Michael Jackson, and many others.

To support their claims, the record labels created AI-generated songs using highly specific prompts and compared the outputs to original copyrighted music. They documented numerous examples where the AI systems produced songs that directly replicated distinctive melodies, rhythms, and styles from famous recordings. One example involved generating a near-identical version of Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas Is You," while another reproduced Green Day's "American Idiot" complete with original lyrics. The lawsuits were filed in New York against Udio and Massachusetts against Suno, setting up a major legal battle over how generative AI services should handle copyrighted material.
